summaries.summary: Generating natural language descriptions of structured data such as tables has grown with sequence to sequence models that encode tables and generate text.
Human judgment is the only gold standard for text generation, but automatic metrics comparing generated text to references, especially BLEU and ROUGE, are routinely used despite divergent references.

Existing automatic metrics including BLEU correlate poorly with human judgments under divergent references, motivating PARENT, which compares generated text to the table using entailment-based union and intersection.
Table-to-text generation is formalized as producing fluent text from records, with references, evaluation sets, n-grams, and the goal of scores correlating highly with human judgments.
PARENT evaluates each instance separately by computing precision and recall against both the reference and the table.
A prior information extraction evaluation model is limited to basketball tables, so the authors train their own extraction model for the open-domain WikiBio dataset.
The extraction system is a pointer-generator network trained on WikiBio to produce linearized tables, with outputs parsed into tuples and compared to ground truth tables.
The authors define CS, RG, and RG-F metrics from extracted pairs and omit content ordering because their extraction system does not align records to input text.
Experiments compare automatic metrics by correlating their model scores with aggregated human evaluation scores using Pearson correlation.
Main experiments use the automatically constructed WikiBio dataset with many divergent references, with additional results on WebNLG challenge data.
Several WikiBio models of varying quality, mainly neural sequence-to-sequence methods plus a template-based baseline, provide diverse outputs for evaluating automatic metrics.
Models are divided into WikiBio-Systems and WikiBio-Hyperparams, with the latter including 13 PG-Net hyperparameter settings for comparing similar high-quality systems.
Human judgments for 16 WikiBio models plus references used paired comparisons aggregated into real-valued scores with Thurstone's method.
Separate annotations for WikiBio-Systems and WikiBio-Hyperparams used 1100 tables, 8800 pairwise comparisons, and around 500 workers, with references scoring lower than PG-Net.
Text-only comparisons include BLEU, ROUGE, METEOR, CIDEr, and CIDEr-D using publicly available implementations.
Information Extraction based comparisons include the CS, RG, and RG-F metrics.
Text & Table comparisons include BLEU-T, PARENT-W, PARENT-C, and tuned PARENT*-W/C versions.
Bootstrap sampling with 500 iterations over 1100 annotated tables estimates correlation variability, with average correlations reported in Table TABREF37.
Table TABREF37 indicates PARENT significance using bootstrap confidence intervals of correlation differences because William's test has weak power with 4/13 systems.
Reference-only metrics BLEU, ROUGE, METEOR, and CIDEr correlate weakly with human judgments, while BLEU performs best among them and BLEU-T improves it.
CS correlates poorly in the hyperparams category, while RG-F and both PARENT variants achieve highest correlations, with PARENT-W significantly better for systems.
On this dataset, word-overlap entailment correlates higher than co-occurrence, while tuning INLINEFORM0 with human annotations can significantly improve PARENT correlations.
The analysis further examines PARENT-W under different conditions and compares it with other best metrics from Table TABREF37.
Workers labeled whether references were entailed by tables, with 3 independent judgments per pair, majority voting, and only INLINEFORM0 references labeled entailed.
As entailed-example proportions vary, PARENT and RG-F remain stable and highly correlated, whereas BLEU and BLEU-T vary substantially.
Removing entailment probability or Table Recall lowers PARENT-W correlation, showing these components are crucial to its performance.
Both PARENT variants significantly outperform other metrics in instance-level pairwise judgment accuracy, though the best binary accuracy is only INLINEFORM0.
PARENT is tested against WebNLG challenge human ratings for 9 systems on 223 instances describing 1-5 RDF triples with up to 3 references.
Human ratings cover grammaticality, fluency, and semantics, and both PARENT variants are competitive or better in average correlation across all three aspects.
BLEU correlates highest for grammar and fluency, while PARENT does best for semantics, and PARENT-C is better than PARENT-W on grammaticality and fluency.
The INLINEFORM0 parameter controls recall against table or reference, with WikiBio relying more on the table and WebNLG more on the reference.
Prior metric evaluations find no single metric suitable across tasks, and this study first checks metric quality when table-to-text references are divergent.
Divergence is framed as hallucination in the reference text, and PARENT discounts n-grams overlapping neither the reference nor the table.
PARENT is inspired by iBLEU but rewards source-table matches, and is a task-specific metric similar to SARI and Q-BLEU.
The paper studies automatic evaluation with divergent references, proposes PARENT, evaluates BIBREF1 metrics, finds RG-F effective, and shows PARENT comparable on WebNLG.
Bhuwan Dhingra is supported by Siemens and Google, and the authors thank named collaborators, Google AI Language team members, Sam Wiseman, and reviewers.
For BIBREF1 evaluation, a WikiBio information extraction PG-Net uses bi-directional LSTMs, attention, copying, and linearized table outputs without coverage.
Despite divergent references causing hallucinated false information, the trained system supports evaluation by parsing extracted (attribute, value) pairs and reporting precision, recall and F-score.
Tuned hyperparameters include 200 hidden states, 50000-word vocabularies, Glove embeddings, Adam, dropout, 40-token texts, 120-token tables, beam size 8 and no length penalty.
Table TABREF55 shows sample references and corresponding predictions from the best performing model, PG-Net for WikiBio.
